vignette:
**Patient Vignette: Mr. K.**

Mr. K. is an 80-year-old widower of South Eastern Asian descent, a retired data scientist who now lives alone in a quiet suburban condominium. He presents as meticulously dressed, his posture rigid, his gaze often fixed on a point just past my shoulder. He speaks with the precision of a man who has spent a lifetime parsing complex datasets, but his sentences are punctuated by long, hollow silences.

He begins his story not in a war zone, but in a sterile, climate-controlled office in the late 1970s. He was a young, brilliant statistician for an international aid organization. His work was abstract: modeling refugee flows, optimizing supply chains for food and medicine. He felt a sense of cosmic purpose, translating human suffering into neat columns of numbers so that help could arrive faster. Then, in 1979, his organization asked for a volunteer to oversee a new data collection system on the ground in a conflict-ravaged region bordering his home country. He saw it as a duty, a chance to see his data become flesh and blood.

He remembers the exact moment the abstraction shattered. He was in a makeshift camp, a sea of tarpaulins and dust. A young mother, clutching an infant, thrust a piece of paper at him—a tattered vaccination record. She was begging, but he didn’t speak her dialect. As he fumbled for a translator, a mortar shell screamed overhead. The world became a deafening, concussive slap. He woke up buried under the canvas of a collapsed tent, the woman’s hand, still clutching the paper, lying inches from his face. The baby was silent.

He stayed for three more months. He tells me he had to. The data was incomplete. He worked 18-hour days, sleeping on a cot in a concrete bunker. He stopped feeling fear; it was replaced by a cold, mechanical focus. He catalogued the dead, the displaced, the missing. He learned to identify the different sounds of incoming fire—the whistle of a mortar, the crack of a sniper. He learned to walk with his head down, to never make eye contact with the soldiers at the checkpoints.

When he returned home, he was promoted. He built a life. He married a quiet, patient woman. They had two children. He never spoke of the camp. He threw himself back into his data, building models for famine prediction, for disease outbreak. He told himself the trauma was a price paid, a debt settled. He believed he had processed it as efficiently as a clean algorithm.

Now, 45 years later, the price is due with compound interest. His wife died five years ago. The silence of his condominium is no longer peaceful; it is a vacuum that the camp rushes to fill. He has not slept more than three hours a night in two years. The moment he closes his eyes, the mortar shell screams. He sees the woman’s hand. He hears the silence of the infant.

He now lives by a rigid, self-imposed schedule. He wakes at 4:00 AM, precisely. He brews a single cup of black coffee. He spends the morning on his computer, not running complex regressions, but meticulously organizing his digital photo library by date, location, and facial recognition. It is a compulsion, a desperate attempt to impose order on a world he knows is chaotic. He cannot bear a single notification on his phone. A sudden, unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a pot dropping in the neighbor’s kitchen—makes him flinch so violently he nearly knocks over his chair. He has stopped going to the grocery store because the crowded aisles feel like a refugee camp. He orders everything online.

He has not told his children. They see him as a stoic, brilliant old man. He fears that if he speaks the words, the dam will break, and he will drown in the data of that single, terrible moment. He is not here for a diagnosis. He is here because he has run out of algorithms to contain the chaos. He simply wants to know if the silence will ever stop feeling like a scream.
